hypotheses.title: executeDeposit/executeWithdrawal lack onlyManager modifier
hypotheses.description: `executeDeposit` and `executeWithdrawal` are documented as manager-only operations ("Can only be called by the manager" per surrounding context and the fact that `cancelDeposit`/`cancelWithdrawal` are `onlyManager`), but neither function has the `onlyManager` modifier. Any external caller can invoke them for any user and any fulfilled epoch, forcing settlement of that user's queued deposit/withdrawal at the current epoch state.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker waits until `depositEpoch`/`withdrawalEpoch` has advanced past a victim's queued epoch. 2) Attacker calls `executeDeposit(victim, victimEpoch)` or `executeWithdrawal(victim, victimEpoch)` directly. 3) The function mints/burns virtual shares and transfers assets to the victim (or moves remainder to the next epoch) without the manager's intended sequencing.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized settlement of other users' positions; can be used to grief (force withdrawals at unfavorable epochs, drain `reservedWithdrawalAssets` accounting, front-run manager's intended fulfillment ordering), and combined with reentrancy/ordering can cause wrong accounting and loss of funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add the `onlyManager` modifier to both `executeDeposit` and `executeWithdrawal`.

hypotheses.title: Manager-supplied prices bypass oracle validation via maxPriceDeviation
hypotheses.description: The NAV computation relies on `managerPrices[i].poolPrice`, `token0Price`, and `token1Price` provided by the vault manager in `managerInput`. These manager prices are only checked to be within `maxPriceDeviation` of the TWAP, but the actual position valuation (`Math.getAmountsForLiquidity`) uses the manager-supplied `poolPrice` directly. A manager can supply a price at the edge of the allowed deviation band to inflate or deflate NAV, and since `maxPriceDeviation` is set per-pool in the `PoolInfo` struct (also supplied by the manager in `managerInput`), the manager can set an arbitrarily large deviation.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Manager calls `fulfillDeposits` or `fulfillWithdrawals` with a crafted `managerInput`. 2. In `PoolInfo`, manager sets `maxPriceDeviation` to a huge value (e.g., type(int24).max). 3. Manager supplies `poolPrice`/`token0Price`/`token1Price` far from the real TWAP. 4. The deviation check `Math.abs(managerPrices[i].poolPrice - twapFilter(...)) > pools[i].maxPriceDeviation` passes trivially. 5. NAV is computed with manipulated prices, causing incorrect share issuance or asset disbursement.
hypotheses.impact: Manager can inflate NAV before `fulfillDeposits` to mint fewer shares to depositors, or deflate NAV before `fulfillWithdrawals` to pay out fewer assets. Direct theft of user funds / wrong accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Store `maxPriceDeviation` and `twapWindow` in the accountant's own storage keyed by pool (set by owner), not in the manager-supplied `PoolInfo` struct. Validate that the supplied `PoolInfo` matches the stored configuration.

hypotheses.title: executeDeposit/executeWithdrawal lack access control, anyone can trigger
hypotheses.description: `executeDeposit` and `executeWithdrawal` are declared `external` with no `onlyManager` modifier, unlike `cancelDeposit`, `cancelWithdrawal`, `fulfillDeposits`, and `fulfillWithdrawals`. Any untrusted external actor can call these functions for any user and any fulfilled epoch, forcing the conversion of pending deposits/withdrawals into shares/assets. Because the functions move remainder amounts into `epoch + 1` and mutate `userBasis`, `reservedWithdrawalAssets`, and balances, an attacker can grief users by forcing execution at times the user did not intend, and can chain calls to manipulate the ordering of state transitions.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a fulfilled epoch (epoch < depositEpoch/withdrawalEpoch). 2) Attacker calls `executeDeposit(victim, epoch)` or `executeWithdrawal(victim, epoch)` for any victim. 3) State is mutated: shares minted, basis updated, remainder pushed to next epoch, `reservedWithdrawalAssets` decremented. 4) Attacker repeats for many users to force premature settlement and to drain `reservedWithdrawalAssets` accounting in an order that benefits them (e.g., front-running a manager's intended batch).
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized state transitions; users' pending deposits/withdrawals are settled without consent; `reservedWithdrawalAssets` can be decremented out of order causing underflow/revert DoS on legitimate manager calls; wrong accounting of basis and shares.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `onlyManager` to `executeDeposit` and `executeWithdrawal`, or require `msg.sender == user` (or an authorized delegate) to prevent third-party forced settlement.

hypotheses.title: PoolInfo struct supplied by manager allows oracle address substitution
hypotheses.description: The `PoolInfo[]` array (including `poolOracle`, `oracle0`, `oracle1`, `token0`, `token1`, `pool`) is fully supplied by the manager in `managerInput` and only validated against `vaultPools[vault]` via `keccak256(abi.encode(pools))`. However, `vaultPools` is set by the owner via `updatePoolsHash`, and the hash covers the entire struct including oracle addresses. If the owner has not yet locked the vault (`vaultLocked` is false), or if the hash was set to a malicious configuration, the manager can point oracles to attacker-controlled contracts that return arbitrary TWAP values, making all deviation checks meaningless.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Manager waits for or before `lockVault` is called, or colludes with owner. 2. Manager supplies `PoolInfo` with `poolOracle`/`oracle0`/`oracle1` pointing to a malicious contract returning a chosen tick. 3. `twapFilter` returns the attacker's tick, matching `managerPrices`, so deviation checks pass. 4. NAV is fully controlled by the manager.
hypotheses.impact: Complete control over NAV computation, enabling theft via mispriced deposits/withdrawals.
hypotheses.recommendation: Do not accept oracle addresses from `managerInput`. Store the canonical `PoolInfo` (oracles, tokens, pool) in accountant storage keyed by vault, and only accept `managerPrices` and `tokenIds` from the manager.

hypotheses.title: fulfillWithdrawals subtracts sharesToFulfill from totalSupply but not from balances
hypotheses.description: `fulfillWithdrawals` does `totalSupply = _totalSupply - sharesToFulfill`, but the shares were already burned virtually in `requestWithdrawal` (reducing balances, not totalSupply). This double-counts the reduction: balances were reduced at request time, and totalSupply is reduced at fulfillment time. The invariant `totalSupply == sum(balances)` is broken, and NAV-per-share calculations become inconsistent.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker requests withdrawal (balance reduced, totalSupply unchanged), then waits for fulfillment (totalSupply reduced). The attacker's remaining shares now represent a larger fraction of totalSupply than their balance warrants, allowing them to extract more assets on subsequent withdrawals or deposits.
hypotheses.impact: Dilution of other shareholders, incorrect share pricing, potential vault insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Do not modify `totalSupply` in `fulfillWithdrawals`; instead, reduce it in `requestWithdrawal` alongside `_burnVirtual`, or track a separate virtual supply.

hypotheses.title: No slippage protection on fulfillWithdrawals asset amount
hypotheses.description: `fulfillWithdrawals` accepts `maxAssetsReceived` as a slippage guard, but it is only checked against `assetsReceived` computed from the manager-supplied NAV. Since the manager controls `managerInput` (and thus NAV), the manager can set `maxAssetsReceived` to `type(uint256).max` and supply a manipulated NAV to disburse an arbitrary amount of assets to withdrawing users, draining the vault. The check `if (assetsReceived > maxAssetsReceived) revert` is ineffective when the manager sets both sides.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Manager calls `fulfillWithdrawals` with `maxAssetsReceived = type(uint256).max` and a `managerInput` that inflates NAV. 2. `assetsReceived` is computed from the inflated NAV. 3. Check passes. 4. `reservedWithdrawalAssets` is increased and assets are paid out to withdrawers at inflated values, draining the vault.
hypotheses.impact: Vault insolvency; remaining depositors cannot withdraw their fair share.
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce `maxAssetsReceived` as a hard cap derived from an independent, trusted source (e.g., a user-set minimum-out per withdrawal request), not from manager-supplied NAV.

hypotheses.title: executeDeposit double-clears queuedDeposit and can lose remainder
hypotheses.description: `executeDeposit` sets `queuedDeposit[user][epoch] = 0` twice (once at the top after reading, once near the end). More importantly, the remainder is moved to `epoch + 1` via `queuedDeposit[user][epoch + 1] += uint128(assetsRemaining)`, but `depositEpochState[epoch + 1].assetsDeposited` is NOT incremented. This desynchronizes the per-user queue from the epoch aggregate, so future fulfillments of epoch+1 will compute wrong shares.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker deposits in epoch N, waits for partial fulfillment, then the remainder is moved to epoch N+1 without updating `depositEpochState[N+1].assetsDeposited`. When epoch N+1 is fulfilled, `assetsFulfilled` may exceed `assetsDeposited`, causing division errors or mispriced shares that the attacker can exploit.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong share accounting, potential revert on fulfillment, loss of funds for depositors in the affected epoch.
hypotheses.recommendation: When moving remainder to `epoch + 1`, also increment `depositEpochState[epoch + 1].assetsDeposited` by `assetsRemaining`.

hypotheses.title: executeWithdrawal moves remainder without updating next epoch aggregate
hypotheses.description: Similar to deposits, `executeWithdrawal` moves `sharesRemaining` and `basisRemaining` to `queuedWithdrawal[user][epoch + 1]` but does not increment `withdrawalEpochState[epoch + 1].sharesWithdrawn`. The next epoch's aggregate is therefore understated, so when `fulfillWithdrawals` is called for epoch+1, `sharesToFulfill` may exceed `sharesWithdrawn`, causing division by zero or incorrect proration.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker requests withdrawal in epoch N, gets partial fulfillment, remainder moves to N+1 without aggregate update. When N+1 is fulfilled, `sharesWithdrawn` is too low, so `sharesToFulfill / sharesWithdrawn` over-prorates, letting the attacker (or other users) claim more assets than deserved.
hypotheses.impact: Over-payment of withdrawals, insolvency of reserved assets, loss to remaining shareholders.
hypotheses.recommendation: Increment `withdrawalEpochState[epoch + 1].sharesWithdrawn` by `sharesRemaining` when moving the remainder.

hypotheses.title: fulfillDeposits adds sharesReceived to totalSupply but shares already minted virtually
hypotheses.description: `fulfillDeposits` does `totalSupply = _totalSupply + sharesReceived`, but `executeDeposit` mints shares virtually via `_mintVirtual` (increasing balances without totalSupply). The comment says "shares from pending deposits are already added to the supply at the start of every new epoch", but the code adds them again at fulfillment. This double-counts shares in totalSupply relative to balances.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker deposits, waits for fulfillment (totalSupply inflated), then requests withdrawal. The inflated totalSupply makes their shares appear worth less, but they can exploit the mismatch by timing deposits/withdrawals across epochs to extract value from the inflated supply.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect share pricing, dilution, potential insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Reconcile the virtual supply model: either mint to totalSupply in `executeDeposit` or in `fulfillDeposits`, but not both.

hypotheses.title: requestWithdrawal divides by zero when user has no shares
hypotheses.description: `requestWithdrawal` computes `withdrawalBasis = (previousBasis * shares) / userBalance` without checking `userBalance > 0`. Any caller with zero shares (or a fresh address) can call `requestWithdrawal(0)` or any amount, causing a division-by-zero revert. More importantly, a user with shares but zero basis (e.g., after a full basis transfer) can be forced into a revert path, and the function lacks any validation that `shares <= balanceOf[msg.sender]`, so `_burnVirtual` can underflow.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `requestWithdrawal(1)` from an address with `balanceOf == 0`. 2) `userBalance == 0` triggers division-by-zero revert (DoS on any integrator that batches calls). 3) Alternatively, a user with shares but `userBasis == 0` cannot withdraw without reverting, and a user can request more shares than they hold, causing `_burnVirtual` underflow.
hypotheses.impact: Denial of service for withdrawal requests; users with zero basis are permanently unable to withdraw; potential underflow reverts bricking withdrawal flow.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `shares > 0 && shares <= balanceOf[msg.sender]` and handle `userBalance == 0` explicitly before computing basis.

hypotheses.title: fulfillDeposits/fulfillWithdrawals lack validation on assetsToFulfill/sharesToFulfill
hypotheses.description: `fulfillDeposits` computes `assetsRemaining = epochState.assetsDeposited - assetsToFulfill` without checking `assetsToFulfill <= assetsDeposited`, causing underflow revert if exceeded (DoS), and `sharesReceived` can be arbitrarily large if `totalAssets` is small (division rounding). Similarly `fulfillWithdrawals` computes `sharesRemaining = epochState.sharesWithdrawn - sharesToFulfill` without bounds check, and `assetsReceived` uses `totalAssets` which can be manipulated. A manager (or anyone if the modifier is missing elsewhere) can pass values that break accounting.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Call `fulfillDeposits(assetsToFulfill > assetsDeposited)` → underflow revert (DoS). 2) Call with `assetsToFulfill` such that `totalAssets` is tiny → `sharesReceived` explodes, diluting existing holders. 3) `fulfillWithdrawals` with `sharesToFulfill > sharesWithdrawn` → underflow revert.
hypotheses.impact: DoS on epoch advancement; share dilution; wrong accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `assetsToFulfill <= epochState.assetsDeposited` and `sharesToFulfill <= epochState.sharesWithdrawn`, and bound `sharesReceived`/`assetsReceived` by sane limits.

hypotheses.title: First depositor / donation attack via virtual share inflation
hypotheses.description: The vault mints shares based on `sharesReceived = assetsToFulfill * totalSupply / totalAssets`, where `totalAssets = NAV + 1 - assetsDeposited - reservedWithdrawalAssets`. The `+1` is a weak offset and the initial `totalSupply = 1_000_000` is set in the constructor with no corresponding assets. An attacker can donate underlying tokens directly to the vault (or via `manage`) to inflate NAV before the first `fulfillDeposits`, causing subsequent depositors to receive far fewer shares than expected, or the attacker can be the sole depositor and capture disproportionate share value.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker is the first to call `requestDeposit` with a tiny amount (e.g., 1 wei). 2) Manager calls `fulfillDeposits` — attacker receives shares based on `totalSupply=1_000_000` and `totalAssets≈1`. 3) Attacker transfers a large amount of underlying directly to the vault (donation), inflating NAV. 4) Next depositor's `fulfillDeposits` computes shares using inflated `totalAssets`, so they receive near-zero shares. 5) Attacker redeems and captures the victim's deposit.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of funds for subsequent depositors; attacker steals deposits via share dilution.
hypotheses.recommendation: Mint a minimum initial share amount to a burn address and/or use a virtual offset (e.g., OpenZeppelin ERC4626-style `+1` on both supply and assets) that is robust to donations; consider locking the first deposit.

hypotheses.title: Missing sequencer uptime / staleness check on TWAP oracles
hypotheses.description: `PanopticMath.twapFilter(pools[i].poolOracle, pools[i].twapWindow)` is called without verifying that the underlying oracle has been updated recently or that the L2 sequencer is up. If the oracle is stale (e.g., no swaps for a long period, or sequencer downtime on L2), the TWAP returns an outdated price. The only protection is the deviation check against `managerPrices`, but the manager controls those prices, so a stale oracle combined with a manager-supplied price within the (manager-controlled) deviation band allows stale prices to be used.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. On an L2 with sequencer downtime, or on a pool with no recent swaps, the oracle TWAP is stale. 2. Manager supplies `managerPrices` matching the stale TWAP. 3. Deviation check passes. 4. NAV is computed using stale prices, mispricing deposits/withdrawals.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect NAV leading to unfair share issuance or asset disbursement; users can be diluted or underpaid.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a sequencer uptime feed check and a staleness check (e.g., `updatedAt` within a max age) before using the TWAP. Also enforce a minimum `twapWindow`.

hypotheses.title: fulfillDeposits/fulfillWithdrawals trust manager-supplied NAV with no signature
hypotheses.description: `computeNAV` accepts `managerInput` containing `ManagerPrices` (poolPrice, token0Price, token1Price) and `PoolInfo` structs directly from the caller. The only validation is that `keccak256(abi.encode(pools)) == vaultPools[vault]` and that manager prices are within `maxPriceDeviation` of the oracle TWAP. However, `PoolInfo` includes `poolOracle`, `oracle0`, `oracle1`, `twapWindow`, and `maxPriceDeviation` fields that are part of the hashed struct — but the hash is set by the owner via `updatePoolsHash`, so the manager cannot swap oracles. The real issue is that `managerPrices[i].poolPrice` is used directly in `Math.getAmountsForLiquidity` to compute position values, and only checked against the TWAP within `maxPriceDeviation`. A manager (or anyone calling `fulfillDeposits`/`fulfillWithdrawals` since those are `onlyManager`) can pick the extreme edge of the allowed deviation to inflate or deflate NAV, minting more shares to depositors or paying out more assets to withdrawers than fair.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Manager calls `fulfillDeposits` with `managerInput` where `poolPrice` is at the boundary `twap ± maxPriceDeviation`. 2) `computeNAV` returns an inflated NAV. 3) `sharesReceived = assetsToFulfill * totalSupply / totalAssets` — with inflated totalAssets, sharesReceived is smaller, but with deflated NAV, sharesReceived is larger. 4) Manager times deposits/withdrawals to extract value from the vault at the expense of other users.
hypotheses.impact: NAV manipulation within the deviation band; dilution of existing shareholders or over-payment to withdrawers; loss of funds to the vault.
hypotheses.recommendation: Tighten `maxPriceDeviation` to a very small value, or require manager prices to be signed/committed off-chain and verified on-chain, or use only oracle TWAP without manager input for pricing.

hypotheses.title: Performance fee can be avoided by transferring shares to a new address before withdrawal
hypotheses.description: When a user requests a withdrawal, `withdrawalBasis = (previousBasis * shares) / userBalance`. If the user transfers shares to a new address (with zero basis) and then requests withdrawal from that new address, the basis is zero, so the entire withdrawal amount is treated as profit, and the performance fee is charged on the full amount. This is the opposite of evasion—it overcharges. However, the attacker can instead transfer shares to an address that already has a high basis (e.g., by depositing a small amount at a high NAV), then request withdrawal. The basis per share is diluted, reducing the apparent profit and thus the fee. By carefully choosing the recipient address's basis, the attacker can minimize the performance fee. This is a classic basis manipulation attack.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker holds shares with low basis (bought cheap). 2) Attacker creates a second address and deposits a tiny amount at a high NAV to establish a high basis. 3) Attacker transfers shares to the second address. 4) The second address's `userBasis` is now high, so when withdrawing, `withdrawnBasis` is high, reducing the profit and the performance fee. 5) Attacker pays less fee than owed.
hypotheses.impact: Performance fee evasion, loss of protocol revenue.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track basis per share using a global accumulator or prevent transfers to addresses with existing basis.

hypotheses.title: fulfillDeposits/fulfillWithdrawals use stale totalSupply for share math
hypotheses.description: `fulfillDeposits` computes `sharesReceived = assetsToFulfill * totalSupply / totalAssets` using the current `totalSupply`, but pending deposit shares are only added to `totalSupply` at fulfillment time. Meanwhile `requestWithdrawal` calls `_burnVirtual` which reduces user balances without reducing `totalSupply`, so `totalSupply` diverges from the sum of balances. The NAV/share calculation is therefore inconsistent between deposits and withdrawals, allowing value extraction.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker requests a large withdrawal (burning virtual shares, reducing their balance but not totalSupply), then waits for a deposit fulfillment. The inflated totalSupply causes new depositors to receive fewer shares than fair, and the attacker's remaining shares are worth more. Alternatively, attacker times deposits/withdrawals around epoch transitions to arbitrage the mismatch.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect share issuance, dilution of honest depositors, potential insolvency of the vault.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track a separate `virtualSupply` that includes pending deposit shares and excludes pending withdrawal shares, and use it consistently in both fulfill functions.

hypotheses.title: cancelDeposit/cancelWithdrawal allow manager to grief users by moving funds
hypotheses.description: `cancelDeposit` and `cancelWithdrawal` are `onlyManager` and allow the manager to cancel any user's pending deposit or withdrawal in the current epoch, refunding assets or re-minting shares. The manager can cancel a user's deposit right before a favorable epoch fulfillment, forcing the user to re-request in a later epoch at a worse price. Similarly, `cancelWithdrawal` re-mints shares and restores basis, but the manager can do this to prevent a user from exiting at a favorable NAV. There is no user consent or timelock.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User requests deposit in epoch N. 2) Manager sees the epoch will be fulfilled at a favorable price. 3) Manager calls `cancelDeposit(user)` to refund the user's assets, preventing them from receiving shares at the favorable price. 4) Manager re-deposits their own funds to capture the favorable price.
hypotheses.impact: Users are denied favorable entries/exits; manager can front-run user requests; loss of expected returns.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require user consent for cancellation (e.g., user must sign a cancellation request), or add a timelock/epoch delay before cancellation takes effect.

hypotheses.title: executeWithdrawal division by zero when sharesWithdrawn is zero
hypotheses.description: In `executeWithdrawal`, `sharesToFulfill` is computed as `pendingWithdrawal.amount * _withdrawalEpochState.sharesFulfilled / _withdrawalEpochState.sharesWithdrawn`. If `sharesWithdrawn` is zero (e.g., all withdrawals in the epoch were cancelled via `cancelWithdrawal`, which decrements `sharesWithdrawn`), this division reverts. Similarly, `withdrawnBasis` divides by `sharesWithdrawn`. A user with a pending withdrawal in an epoch where all shares were cancelled cannot execute their withdrawal, and their funds are frozen.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. User requests withdrawal in epoch N. 2. Manager calls `cancelWithdrawal` on all other withdrawers in epoch N, bringing `sharesWithdrawn` to zero (or the user's own amount is the only one and gets cancelled). 3. `fulfillWithdrawals` is called with `sharesToFulfill = 0`, setting `sharesFulfilled = 0`. 4. User calls `executeWithdrawal`; division by zero reverts. 5. User's shares are burned but assets are never returned.
hypotheses.impact: Frozen funds; user cannot retrieve assets after requesting withdrawal.
hypotheses.recommendation: Guard against `sharesWithdrawn == 0` and `sharesFulfilled == 0` by returning early or handling the zero case explicitly.

hypotheses.title: fulfillDeposits/fulfillWithdrawals trust manager-supplied accountant input
hypotheses.description: `fulfillDeposits` and `fulfillWithdrawals` pass `managerInput` directly to `accountant.computeNAV`, which decodes arbitrary `PoolInfo` structs including `pool`, `token0`, `token1`, oracles, and `maxPriceDeviation`. The accountant only checks `keccak256(abi.encode(pools)) == vaultPools[vault]`, but the manager controls the entire input and can supply a `pools` array whose hash matches while still influencing NAV via `managerPrices` (which are only bounded by `maxPriceDeviation` chosen by the manager in the same input). A malicious or compromised manager can inflate/deflate NAV to mint shares cheaply or drain withdrawals.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Manager (or anyone who can influence the manager, but per rules the manager is trusted — however the accountant's `updatePoolsHash` is owner-only and `vaultLocked` can be bypassed if not locked) supplies crafted `managerPrices` within `maxPriceDeviation` to skew NAV. 2) Calls `fulfillDeposits` with inflated NAV to mint fewer shares, or `fulfillWithdrawals` with deflated NAV to underpay withdrawers. 3) Since `maxPriceDeviation` is part of the manager-supplied `PoolInfo`, the manager can set it arbitrarily large.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong share pricing, theft from depositors/withdrawers, vault insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Store `maxPriceDeviation` and pool configs in the accountant (owner-set, not manager-supplied) and validate `managerPrices` against on-chain oracles with a fixed deviation bound.

hypotheses.title: Fee-on-transfer / rebasing tokens break deposit and NAV accounting
hypotheses.description: `requestDeposit` credits `queuedDeposit[msg.sender][currentEpoch] += assets` and `depositEpochState[currentEpoch].assetsDeposited += assets` based on the requested `assets` amount, not the actual received amount. If `underlyingToken` is fee-on-transfer or rebasing, the vault's real balance is less than the recorded `assetsDeposited`, so `fulfillDeposits` computes shares against inflated assets, diluting existing holders. Similarly, `cancelDeposit` refunds the full recorded amount, potentially draining more than was received.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deposits a fee-on-transfer token; vault records full `assets` but receives less. 2) `fulfillDeposits` mints shares as if full assets were received, diluting other holders. 3) Attacker can also `cancelDeposit` to receive the full recorded amount, extracting more than deposited.
hypotheses.impact: Insolvency / dilution of existing depositors; vault balance drifts from recorded accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Measure the actual balance delta in `requestDeposit` and use that for accounting; document and restrict supported tokens to non-fee-on-transfer, non-rebasing.

hypotheses.title: fulfillDeposits/fulfillWithdrawals use NAV before accounting for pending flows
hypotheses.description: In `fulfillDeposits`, `totalAssets` is computed as `NAV + 1 - epochState.assetsDeposited - reservedWithdrawalAssets`. The `+1` is a rounding guard, but the subtraction of `epochState.assetsDeposited` assumes all pending deposits are still held as underlying in the vault. If the manager has already deployed those assets (via `manage`) into positions, the NAV already reflects them, and subtracting `assetsDeposited` double-counts the outflow, understating `totalAssets` and inflating `sharesReceived`. This lets the manager manipulate share issuance.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Manager deploys pending deposit assets into a position via `manage`. 2. Manager calls `fulfillDeposits` with a small `assetsToFulfill`. 3. `totalAssets` is understated because `assetsDeposited` is subtracted even though those assets are already in NAV. 4. `sharesReceived = assetsToFulfill * totalSupply / totalAssets` is inflated. 5. Depositors receive more shares than fair, diluting existing holders.
hypotheses.impact: Dilution of existing shareholders; incorrect share accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Clarify whether pending deposits are held as idle underlying or deployed. If deployed, do not subtract `assetsDeposited` from NAV; if idle, ensure the manager cannot deploy them before fulfillment.

hypotheses.title: requestDeposit state updated before transferFrom enables reentrant double-count
hypotheses.description: `queuedDeposit`, `depositEpochState.assetsDeposited` are incremented before `SafeTransferLib.safeTransferFrom`. If the underlying token has a callback (ERC-777 or malicious ERC-20), the recipient can reenter `requestDeposit`, `requestWithdrawal`, or `cancelDeposit`-adjacent views and observe falsely-inflated epoch accounting before the actual assets arrive. The state-increment-before-transfer order lets an attacker double-count their deposit in the epoch state during the callback window.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker deploys/uses a callback-enabled underlying (or calls via a hook that notifies on transferFrom). On transfer, attacker reenters `requestDeposit` while the first call's state is already written, causing `depositEpochState.assetsDeposited` to reflect 2× assets for a single token movement, or worse, reenters `executeDeposit`/`fulfillDeposits` if epoch boundaries line up during the window.
hypotheses.impact: Mis-attributed epoch accounting allowing excess shares payout from fulfilled deposits (protocol drains later fulfillments); insolvency of the vault's deposit queue.
hypotheses.recommendation: Perform the `safeTransferFrom` before mutating `queuedDeposit`/`depositEpochState`, or add a reentrancy guard on all state-mutating vault entrypoints.

hypotheses.title: fulfillWithdrawals maxAssetsReceived check is bypassable via NAV manipulation
hypotheses.description: `fulfillWithdrawals` computes `assetsReceived = sharesToFulfill * totalAssets / totalSupply` and checks `assetsReceived > maxAssetsReceived` reverts. However, `totalAssets` is derived from `accountant.computeNAV(...)` which uses manager-supplied prices. The manager can set `maxAssetsReceived` to `type(uint256).max` (or a very high value) and manipulate `managerInput` prices to inflate `totalAssets`, causing `assetsReceived` to be larger than fair, draining `reservedWithdrawalAssets` and the vault's underlying balance. Since the manager is the caller, this is a self-dealing vector, but the check is meant to protect the vault — it does not, because the manager controls both sides.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Manager calls `fulfillWithdrawals(sharesToFulfill, type(uint256).max, managerInput)` with `managerInput` prices at the high end of the deviation band. 2) `computeNAV` returns inflated `totalAssets`. 3) `assetsReceived` is inflated. 4) `reservedWithdrawalAssets` is incremented by the inflated amount, and later `executeWithdrawal` pays out the inflated amount to the withdrawer (who may be the manager or a colluder).
hypotheses.impact: Over-payment to withdrawers; depletion of vault assets; `reservedWithdrawalAssets` accounting inflated, causing future `fulfillWithdrawals` to underflow or revert.
hypotheses.recommendation: Do not rely on manager-supplied `maxAssetsReceived`; enforce a hard cap based on oracle-only NAV, or require the manager to commit to `maxAssetsReceived` off-chain with a signature.

hypotheses.title: Performance fee basis manipulation via share transfer to fresh address
hypotheses.description: `_transferBasis` transfers a proportional share of `userBasis` when shares move, but if the recipient already has shares with a lower basis, the transferred basis is simply added. More critically, a user can transfer shares to a fresh address (basis 0) and then request a withdrawal from that address; the withdrawal basis is computed as `(previousBasis * shares) / userBalance`, which for the fresh address equals the transferred basis. However, the attacker can instead transfer shares to an address that already holds shares with a very low basis, diluting the effective basis and reducing the performance fee owed on withdrawal. The basis accounting is per-address and can be gamed by splitting/merging share positions across addresses to minimize the computed `withdrawnBasis`, thereby minimizing the performance fee.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker holds shares with high basis (bought at high NAV). 2) Attacker transfers shares to a second address that already holds a tiny amount of shares with near-zero basis. 3) The `_transferBasis` adds the high basis to the second address, but the second address's `userBasis` per share is now diluted. 4) Attacker requests withdrawal from the second address; `withdrawalBasis = (previousBasis * shares) / userBalance` yields a lower basis per share than the true cost, inflating the apparent profit and... actually inflating the fee. The inverse: attacker can transfer shares to an address with high basis to reduce apparent profit and pay less fee. By choosing the recipient's existing basis, the attacker controls the computed `withdrawnBasis` and thus the performance fee.
hypotheses.impact: Performance fees can be systematically underpaid (fee evasion), reducing protocol revenue; or overpaid, harming users. The basis accounting is not robust to address splitting/merging.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track basis per share using a global accumulator (e.g., average cost basis per share) rather than per-address proportional transfer, or forbid transfers to addresses with existing basis.

hypotheses.title: requestWithdrawal divides by userBalance allowing zero-balance revert or basis theft
hypotheses.description: `withdrawalBasis = (previousBasis * shares) / userBalance` divides by `balanceOf[msg.sender]`. If a user has zero balance (e.g., after a prior withdrawal request burned all shares) but nonzero `userBasis` (from a prior deposit that hasn't been executed), calling `requestWithdrawal` reverts. More critically, if `userBalance` is small relative to `previousBasis` (e.g., after partial transfers), the basis calculation can be manipulated.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker transfers most shares away (basis transfers proportionally), then requests withdrawal of remaining shares. The basis math can be gamed by transferring shares to a fresh address to reset basis, then withdrawing with zero basis, avoiding performance fees entirely.
hypotheses.impact: Performance fee evasion, incorrect basis accounting, potential revert DoS on legitimate withdrawals.
hypotheses.recommendation: Guard against `userBalance == 0` and ensure basis is tracked per-share consistently; consider using a global share-price basis model.

hypotheses.title: PanopticVaultAccountant.updatePoolsHash can be front-run before lock
hypotheses.description: `updatePoolsHash` is `onlyOwner` and reverts only if `vaultLocked[vault]` is true. Until `lockVault` is called, the owner can change the pools hash at any time, including after a vault has been deployed and users have deposited. There is no timelock or two-step process, so a malicious/compromised owner can swap the pool configuration to one that reports a manipulated NAV.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Vault deployed, users deposit, `vaultPools[vault]` set to legitimate pools. 2) Owner calls `updatePoolsHash(vault, maliciousHash)` before `lockVault`. 3) Manager calls `fulfillDeposits`/`fulfillWithdrawals` with input matching the malicious hash, skewing NAV.
hypotheses.impact: NAV manipulation, theft from vault users, insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `lockVault` to be called atomically with vault setup, or add a timelock on `updatePoolsHash` after first deposit.

hypotheses.title: Rounding in fulfillWithdrawals favors withdrawer over remaining holders
hypotheses.description: `assetsReceived = mulDiv(sharesToFulfill, totalAssets, _totalSupply)` rounds down, but `totalSupply` is reduced by exactly `sharesToFulfill` while `reservedWithdrawalAssets` is increased by the rounded-down `assetsReceived`. The dust difference between the true proportional value and the rounded value remains in the vault and is effectively redistributed to remaining shareholders. More critically, `executeWithdrawal` computes `sharesToFulfill` and `assetsToWithdraw` with two sequential floor divisions, so a user can be underpaid relative to their true pro-rata claim, and the leftover basis/shares are pushed to the next epoch where they may be diluted.
hypotheses.attackPath: A withdrawer requests a withdrawal sized so that `sharesToFulfill * assetsReceived / sharesFulfilled` truncates to a value below their fair share; the dust accumulates in the vault and is captured by other users (or the manager via subsequent fulfillments). Repeated small withdrawals amplify the truncation loss.
hypotheses.impact: Withdrawers systematically lose small amounts to rounding; accounting drift between `reservedWithdrawalAssets` and actual obligations.
hypotheses.recommendation: Round `assetsReceived` up when fulfilling withdrawals, or track the exact residual and credit it back to the epoch; use a single mulDiv for the final asset amount.

hypotheses.title: executeWithdrawal transfers fee before user, but reads then mutates reservedWithdrawalAssets across calls
hypotheses.description: `reservedWithdrawalAssets` is decremented and `queuedWithdrawal` is cleared, then two `safeTransfer` calls fire to `feeWallet` and `user`. A callback-on-transfer underlying token can reenter `executeWithdrawal` for a different epoch/user (or `fulfillWithdrawals`) mid-flight. More critically, `queuedWithdrawal[user][epoch]` is cleared *after* reads of pendingWithdrawal but the payout path calls out before the state is fully settled for the user, enabling reentrancy against the same `epoch+1` bucket while the outer call's payout is still pending.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker with callback token requests withdrawal; manager calls executeWithdrawal; during the fee/user transfer callback, attacker reenters `executeWithdrawal` with a second identity or `cancelWithdrawal` for the still-stale `epoch+1` slot, causing double-mint of virtual shares or double payout.
hypotheses.impact: Duplicate payouts / inflated virtual balances; drains reservedWithdrawalAssets faster than accounting reflects; vault insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Zero out pendingWithdrawal before performing transfers (use cached locals), and/or apply a nonReentrant modifier on executeDeposit/executeWithdrawal/cancelDeposit/cancelWithdrawal/fulfillDeposits/fulfillWithdrawals.

hypotheses.title: cancelDeposit state-update-after-transfer allows reentrant double-refund on callback tokens
hypotheses.description: Reads `queuedDepositAmount`, zeroes the user's queue, subtracts from `depositEpochState.assetsDeposited`, then transfers assets to depositor. Because the transfer is a callback-enabled token (ERC-777 style), the depositor can reenter `cancelDeposit` in the manager's name — actually the attacker cannot call `cancelDeposit` (onlyManager), but can reenter `requestDeposit` (public) mid-transfer and re-add to the same epoch's `assetsDeposited` while the manager's cancellation accounting is already enforced. Worse: any public function (`requestWithdrawal`, `transfer`) invoked during the callback executes against already-mutated state and can observe the depositor's balance before the refund settles.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker is depositor, uses an ERC-777-like underlying. Manager legitimately calls `cancelDeposit(attacker)`. During `safeTransfer` callback, attacker calls `requestWithdrawal` with shares obtained elsewhere, locking in a withdrawal basis computed against the already-decremented epoch state, extracting disproportionate value at fulfillment.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong share/basis accounting; attacker extracts more assets than deposited; vault value leak.
hypotheses.recommendation: Move `SafeTransfer` to after all state writes complete AND add nonReentrant, or use a pull-payment pattern for refunds.

hypotheses.title: fulfillDeposits/fulfillWithdrawals can be frozen by manager, trapping user funds
hypotheses.description: Deposits and withdrawals are only fulfilled when the manager calls fulfillDeposits/fulfillWithdrawals. If the manager stops calling (or is removed via setManager to address(0)), user deposits sit in the vault and withdrawal requests never convert to assets. Users can cancel deposits only via manager (cancelDeposit is onlyManager), so users cannot self-recover their deposited assets. This traps funds indefinitely. The attacker model excludes trusted roles, but the impact is a liveness failure reachable by any manager removal or inaction. Since the manager is trusted, this is borderline; but the user has no self-service escape hatch, which is a design-level DoS.
hypotheses.attackPath: Manager (trusted) stops fulfilling; users cannot cancelDeposit themselves; funds stuck.
hypotheses.impact: User deposits and withdrawal requests frozen indefinitely.
hypotheses.recommendation: Allow users to cancel their own pending deposits/withdrawals in the current epoch, or add a timeout-based escape.

hypotheses.title: fulfillDeposits/fulfillWithdrawals lack deadline and nonce; replayable across epochs
hypotheses.description: `fulfillDeposits` and `fulfillWithdrawals` take `managerInput` bytes with no nonce, deadline, or chain-id binding. While these are `onlyManager`, the manager is a hot key that may sign meta-transactions or relayed calls. More importantly, the `managerInput` is not bound to a specific epoch or vault state, so if the same `managerInput` is reused after state changes (e.g., after a partial fulfillment), the accountant will recompute NAV against the new state and the manager's intended prices may no longer be valid. There is no replay protection if the manager's calls are relayed.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Manager submits `fulfillDeposits(assetsToFulfill, managerInput)` via a relayer. 2) The relayer (or an observer) replays the same calldata in a later block after state has changed. 3) The accountant recomputes NAV with stale manager prices against new pool state, potentially passing the deviation check by coincidence or reverting. 4) If it passes, shares are minted at a stale price.
hypotheses.impact: Stale-price fulfillment; incorrect share/asset amounts; potential value extraction if replay lands in a favorable state.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include a nonce, deadline, and `block.chainid`/`address(this)` in the signed/committed manager input, and verify them in `fulfillDeposits`/`fulfillWithdrawals`.

hypotheses.title: Performance fee basis uses stale userBasis after partial fulfillment
hypotheses.description: `withdrawnBasis` is computed as `pendingWithdrawal.basis * sharesFulfilled / sharesWithdrawn`, and the performance fee is charged on `assetsToWithdraw - withdrawnBasis`. However, `pendingWithdrawal.basis` was set at request time using the user's basis at that moment, and `userBasis` was already decremented then. If the user's shares were partially fulfilled across epochs, the basis carried forward in `queuedWithdrawal[user][epoch+1]` may not reflect the actual cost basis of the remaining shares (e.g., after transfers or additional deposits), leading to over- or under-charging of performance fees. An attacker can manipulate their basis via `transfer`/`transferFrom` (which proportionally moves basis) to minimize the fee.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker acquires shares with high basis (e.g., by depositing at a high NAV). 2) Attacker transfers shares to a fresh address, moving proportional basis. 3) Attacker requests withdrawal from the fresh address; the fee is computed against the transferred basis, which may be lower than the true economic basis, reducing the fee owed. Conversely, a user with low basis can be overcharged.
hypotheses.impact: Fee evasion (protocol revenue loss) or overcharging of users; incorrect performance fee accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute the fee against the actual assets deposited for those shares (track per-epoch basis precisely) rather than a proportional snapshot that can be gamed via transfers.

hypotheses.title: uint128 truncation in deposit/withdrawal epoch state can silently lose funds
hypotheses.description: `depositEpochState[currentEpoch]` stores `assetsDeposited`, `sharesReceived`, and `assetsFulfilled` as `uint128`. `sharesReceived` is computed as a `uint256` and cast to `uint128` without a bounds check. If `assetsToFulfill * totalSupply / totalAssets` exceeds `type(uint128).max` (possible with large TVL or high share price), the cast truncates, and `totalSupply` is incremented by the truncated value while `depositEpochState` records the truncated value — but `executeDeposit` uses the truncated `sharesReceived` to mint, so users receive fewer shares than the supply increase implies, creating a mismatch. Similarly, `assetsReceived` in `fulfillWithdrawals` is cast to `uint128`.
hypotheses.attackPath: An attacker (or natural growth) pushes `sharesReceived` above `2^128-1`; the truncation causes `totalSupply` and per-user minted shares to diverge, and the excess supply is effectively burned/unaccounted, or users are underpaid.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of funds / incorrect share accounting; potential insolvency if withdrawals are computed against a mismatched supply.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `uint256` for epoch state fields, or add explicit `require(value <= type(uint128).max)` checks before casting.

hypotheses.title: Zero-amount deposit/withdrawal and dust edge cases corrupt basis
hypotheses.description: `requestWithdrawal` computes `withdrawalBasis = previousBasis * shares / userBalance`. If `shares == 0`, `withdrawalBasis = 0` and the function still burns 0 shares and records a zero pending withdrawal, which is harmless. But if `userBalance == 0` (e.g., after all shares were burned in a prior request), the division reverts, blocking any further interaction. More subtly, if `shares` is very small relative to `userBalance`, `withdrawalBasis` truncates to 0, so the user's basis is not reduced, and on `executeWithdrawal` the fee is computed against a basis that overstates cost, undercharging the fee. Conversely, `cancelWithdrawal` adds back the recorded basis, which may exceed the original if rounding accumulated.
hypotheses.attackPath: An attacker repeatedly requests tiny withdrawals to accumulate basis drift, then cancels them to inflate `userBasis`, reducing future performance fees on profitable withdrawals.
hypotheses.impact: Performance fee evasion; incorrect basis accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Reject zero-share withdrawals and ensure basis is reduced proportionally with rounding that favors the protocol (round basis down, not up).

hypotheses.title: Accountant computeNAV is read-only but manager controls managerInput, enabling same-block NAV manipulation
hypotheses.description: `computeNAV` trusts `managerPrices[i]` supplied by the manager, only checking against a TWAP with `twapWindow`. A short TWAP window combined with the manager choosing exactly what poolPrice to submit allows the manager to accept near-spot prices, effectively letting a same-block manipulator sandwich the pool to move NAV within tolerance, then call `fulfillWithdrawals`/`fulfillDeposits` in the same block. Because `fulfillWithdrawals` mints `assetsReceived` from NAV-totalSupply, a small NAV shift swings owed assets disproportionately when totalAssets is small.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker (anyone with balance to sandwich and knowledge of pending fulfillment) manipulates the pool price within `maxPriceDeviation` of the TWAP, then triggers/waits for a `fulfillWithdrawals`/`fulfillDeposits` tx in the same block, causing mispriced share issuance or mispriced asset distribution.
hypotheses.impact: Users receive incorrect shares/assets; value transfer between depositors and withdrawers at fulfillment; possible vault insolvency from over-issued shares.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require TWAP window sufficiently long, enforce TWAP consistency via an on-chain check independent of manager input, and disallow fulfillment in the same block as the price-mutating trade that shifted the TWAP.

hypotheses.title: fulfillWithdrawals cross-function reentrancy via accountant.computeNAV managerInput callback
hypotheses.description: `accountant.computeNAV(address(this), underlyingToken, managerInput)` is called with entirely manager-controlled data. The accountant will call external contracts (`pool.getAccumulatedFeesAndPositionsData`, oracles, `previewRedeem`, `balanceOf`). A malicious/compromised accountant (owner-set) is excluded, but the accountant itself calls into third-party pools/tokens. If any of those tokens is callback-enabled (e.g., `previewRedeem` on a malicious ERC-4626) it can reenter `fulfillWithdrawals`/`fulfillDeposits`/`requestWithdrawal` before `withdrawalEpoch` and `reservedWithdrawalAssets` are updated. The state mutations in `fulfillWithdrawals` (epochState write, epoch bump, totalSupply reduce, reservedWithdrawalAssets increase) all happen *after* the NAV computation, giving the callback a window on stale state.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker deploys a malicious vault/pool whose collateral token's `previewRedeem` reverts or callbacks. Manager's fulfillment tx triggers the callback mid-NAV; attacker reenters with `requestWithdrawal` on the same block, locking shares from the still-stale `totalSupply` and `withdrawalEpochState`, then exits before the epoch bump takes effect.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker captures more assets at the new epoch than shares entitle; drains reservedWithdrawalAssets; partial vault insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add nonReentrant to fulfill* and execute*, and snapshot `withdrawalEpoch`/`depositEpoch` at function start so reentrancy uses fresh values.

hypotheses.title: requestWithdrawal division by zero when userBalance is zero (reentrancy or direct)
hypotheses.description: `withdrawalBasis = (previousBasis * shares) / userBalance` reverts if `userBalance == 0`, and `_burnVirtual` also reverts. However, a reentrant ERC-721-style transfer or `transferFrom` callback during a previous call can move the attacker's shares out while `queuedWithdrawal` state is being assembled, leaving the attacker able to interleave reads so that `userBasis[msg.sender]` is recomputed against a stale `balanceOf`. More importantly, the ordering `userBasis` write, then `queuedWithdrawal` write, then `withdrawalEpochState.sharesWithdrawn` write, then `_burnVirtual`, all happen without a guard — a callback token hit during a later `safeTransfer` from another function can observe partial state where shares are queued but not burned.
hypotheses.attackPath: If underlying is a callback token, deposit→cancel→reentrant requestWithdrawal sequence during transfer callback can reach requestWithdrawal with a partially updated `userBasis` and `balanceOf` mismatch, producing an incorrect basis for the queued withdrawal, which after fulfillment pays out more than the user's cost basis implies.
hypotheses.impact: Over-payment of assets at fulfillment (fee bypass or basis inflation extracting more assets); frozen funds if state becomes inconsistent.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a reentrancy guard, and compute basis against a cached `balanceOf` snapshot before any writes in the same tx.

hypotheses.title: executeWithdrawal can underflow reservedWithdrawalAssets if assetsToWithdraw > reserved
hypotheses.description: executeWithdrawal computes assetsToWithdraw = sharesToFulfill * assetsReceived / sharesFulfilled, then reservedWithdrawalAssets -= assetsToWithdraw. If assetsToWithdraw > reservedWithdrawalAssets, this underflows and reverts. Can this happen? reservedWithdrawalAssets is incremented by assetsReceived in fulfillWithdrawals. The sum of assetsToWithdraw across all users in an epoch should equal assetsReceived (since sharesToFulfill sums to sharesFulfilled). But due to rounding, the sum of individual assetsToWithdraw may exceed assetsReceived by a few wei, causing the last user's executeWithdrawal to underflow and revert. This is a real rounding-induced DoS: the last user cannot withdraw, and their funds are stuck. An untrusted attacker cannot directly trigger this, but any user can be the unlucky last one. The attacker could potentially be the last user by timing, but cannot force others. Still, this is a liveness bug affecting users.
hypotheses.attackPath: Rounding causes sum of assetsToWithdraw > reservedWithdrawalAssets; last user's executeWithdrawal reverts, funds stuck.
hypotheses.impact: Last user's withdrawal permanently reverts; funds stuck in vault.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track per-user fulfilled amounts, or use a running total and cap the last withdrawal to remaining reserved.

hypotheses.title: executeWithdrawal casts sharesRemaining and basisRemaining to uint128 without check
hypotheses.description: executeWithdrawal casts sharesRemaining and basisRemaining to uint128 when adding to queuedWithdrawal[user][epoch+1]. If the sum exceeds uint128, truncation occurs. Since pendingWithdrawal.amount and .basis are uint128, the sum with nextQueuedWithdrawal (also uint128) can exceed uint128. This is a real overflow: if a user has a pending withdrawal in epoch+1 and a remainder from epoch, the sum can exceed uint128, truncating silently. This corrupts accounting. An attacker could potentially cause this by making many withdrawals across epochs. Permissionless executeWithdrawal can trigger it. This is a real bug.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker (or any user) accumulates withdrawals across epochs; executeWithdrawal truncates the sum, corrupting queued amounts.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong accounting; user may lose funds or receive too much.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use uint256 for queued amounts, or check for overflow before casting.

hypotheses.title: Withdrawal epoch basis proration ignores unfulfilled shares leading to fee miscalculation
hypotheses.description: In `executeWithdrawal`, `withdrawnBasis` is prorated by `sharesFulfilled / sharesWithdrawn`, but the remaining basis is moved to the next epoch. If the manager fulfills only a fraction of shares, the basis carried forward is `pendingWithdrawal.basis - withdrawnBasis`. However, the performance fee is computed on `assetsToWithdraw - withdrawnBasis`. If the epoch's `assetsReceived` is disproportionately high relative to `sharesFulfilled` (e.g., due to NAV manipulation or timing), the fee can be computed on an inflated profit. More importantly, if `sharesFulfilled` is 0 (manager fulfills 0 shares), the division `assetsReceived / sharesFulfilled` in the next line would revert, but the check `epoch >= withdrawalEpoch` prevents executing the current epoch. The real issue: the basis proration uses `sharesFulfilled / sharesWithdrawn`, but `sharesWithdrawn` includes shares from users who may have cancelled or whose shares were moved. If a user's shares are partially fulfilled across epochs, the basis accounting can drift, leading to incorrect fee calculation.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker requests withdrawal of a large amount of shares. 2) Manager fulfills a small fraction. 3) Attacker's basis is prorated, but the remaining basis is moved to the next epoch. 4) Attacker can then cancel the withdrawal in the next epoch (if manager allows) to restore basis, or execute again. By timing fulfillment and cancellations, the attacker can manipulate the basis to minimize fees.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect performance fee calculation, potential fee evasion or overcharging.
hypotheses.recommendation: Ensure basis proration is consistent and cannot be gamed by partial fulfillment; consider tracking basis per share globally.

hypotheses.title: Reserved withdrawal assets can be double-counted in NAV calculation
hypotheses.description: In `fulfillDeposits`, `totalAssets = accountant.computeNAV(...) + 1 - epochState.assetsDeposited - reservedWithdrawalAssets`. The `reservedWithdrawalAssets` are assets set aside for fulfilled withdrawals. However, the accountant's `computeNAV` includes the vault's token balances, which include the reserved assets. Subtracting `reservedWithdrawalAssets` from NAV is correct to avoid double-counting, but if the reserved assets are held in a different form (e.g., invested), the subtraction may be incorrect. More critically, in `fulfillWithdrawals`, `totalAssets = accountant.computeNAV(...) + 1 - depositEpochState[depositEpoch].assetsDeposited - _reservedWithdrawalAssets`. Here, `_reservedWithdrawalAssets` is the current reserved amount, but the NAV already includes those assets. Subtracting them again could understate NAV, leading to fewer shares minted for deposits or fewer assets for withdrawals. This can be exploited by timing deposits/withdrawals around fulfillment.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deposits before a large withdrawal fulfillment. 2) The NAV is understated due to double subtraction of reserved assets. 3) Attacker's deposit gets more shares than fair. 4) Attacker withdraws after, profiting from the dilution.
hypotheses.impact: Dilution of existing shareholders, unfair share distribution.
hypotheses.recommendation: Ensure reserved assets are not double-counted; consider tracking them separately from NAV.

hypotheses.title: setManager to address(0) bricks vault, trapping all funds
hypotheses.description: setManager is onlyOwner. If the owner sets manager to address(0) (or a non-functional address), then fulfillDeposits, fulfillWithdrawals, cancelDeposit, cancelWithdrawal, and manage become uncallable. Users cannot cancel their own deposits (cancelDeposit is onlyManager), so all deposited assets and pending withdrawals are permanently stuck. This is an owner-triggered DoS, but the rules exclude owner/admin abuse. However, the impact is severe and the code provides no user-side escape hatch. Borderline; excluded per rules.
hypotheses.attackPath: Owner sets manager to address(0); users cannot recover funds.
hypotheses.impact: All funds stuck.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add user-callable cancelDeposit/cancelWithdrawal for current epoch, or a timelock escape.

hypotheses.title: executeDeposit division by zero when assetsDeposited is zero
hypotheses.description: executeDeposit computes userAssetsDeposited = queuedDepositAmount * assetsFulfilled / assetsDeposited. If assetsDeposited is zero (epoch with no deposits), this reverts. But if assetsDeposited is zero, queuedDepositAmount is also zero, so the call is a no-op but still reverts. An attacker can call executeDeposit for any user/epoch where assetsDeposited=0 to cause a revert, but only their own tx reverts. Not a griefing vector against others. Low impact.
hypotheses.attackPath: User calls executeDeposit for empty epoch; own tx reverts.
hypotheses.impact: Self-DoS only.
hypotheses.recommendation: Guard with `if (assetsDeposited == 0) return;`.

hypotheses.title: queuedDeposit and queuedWithdrawal use uint128, can overflow with many small deposits
hypotheses.description: queuedDeposit[user][epoch] is uint128. requestDeposit does queuedDeposit[msg.sender][currentEpoch] += assets, where assets is uint128. If a user makes many deposits in the same epoch, the sum can overflow uint128, reverting. This is self-inflicted (user's own deposits), but an attacker could grief a specific user by sending them tokens? No, deposits are from msg.sender. So only self-DoS. Low impact.
hypotheses.attackPath: User deposits repeatedly until uint128 overflow; own tx reverts.
hypotheses.impact: Self-DoS only.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use uint256 for queued amounts.

hypotheses.title: queuedWithdrawal amount and basis use uint128, can overflow
hypotheses.description: queuedWithdrawal[user][epoch].amount and .basis are uint128. requestWithdrawal adds shares and withdrawalBasis. If a user makes many withdrawals in the same epoch, the sum can overflow uint128, reverting. Self-inflicted. Low impact.
hypotheses.attackPath: User withdraws repeatedly until uint128 overflow; own tx reverts.
hypotheses.impact: Self-DoS only.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use uint256 for queued amounts.

hypotheses.title: Deposit epoch share calculation uses totalSupply that excludes pending deposits, allowing dilution
hypotheses.description: In `fulfillDeposits`, `sharesReceived = assetsToFulfill * totalSupply / totalAssets`. The `totalSupply` used is the current total supply, which does not include shares from pending deposits in the current epoch (those are minted virtually only when executed). However, `totalAssets` subtracts `epochState.assetsDeposited` (the assets deposited in the current epoch). This means the NAV per share is computed excluding the pending deposits, but the shares minted for those deposits are based on the pre-deposit NAV. If the manager fulfills deposits at a favorable NAV, the new depositors get more shares than they should, diluting existing holders. Conversely, if the manager times fulfillment after a loss, new depositors get fewer shares. The manager (trusted) controls timing, but an attacker can exploit by depositing and then having the manager fulfill at a manipulated NAV. Since the manager is trusted, this is not directly exploitable by an untrusted actor, but the design allows the manager to favor certain depositors.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not directly exploitable by untrusted actor; requires manager collusion.
hypotheses.impact: Dilution of existing shareholders or unfair share distribution.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include pending deposits in the total supply calculation or use a more robust share pricing mechanism.

hypotheses.title: Withdrawal fulfillment can be front-run to manipulate NAV and steal funds
hypotheses.description: `fulfillWithdrawals` computes `assetsReceived = sharesToFulfill * totalAssets / totalSupply`. The `totalAssets` is computed from the accountant's NAV, which depends on `managerInput` provided by the manager. An attacker who is also a depositor can observe the manager's transaction and front-run it by requesting a withdrawal or deposit to manipulate the epoch state. More critically, the `maxAssetsReceived` parameter is set by the manager, but if the manager is compromised or the accountant is manipulable, an attacker can force a large `assetsReceived` by manipulating the NAV via oracle manipulation (if the accountant uses oracles). The accountant checks oracle prices against manager-provided prices, but the manager provides those prices, so a malicious manager can set them to manipulate NAV. Since the manager is trusted, this is not directly exploitable by an untrusted actor, but the oracle deviation check can be bypassed if the manager provides prices within the deviation but still manipulated.
hypotheses.attackPath: Requires manager collusion or oracle manipulation.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of funds from the vault.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a decentralized oracle or time-weighted average price with a longer window; do not rely on manager-provided prices.
